newsitem.title: INDONESIA: At least 200 said killed in Indonesia clashes.
newsitem.headline: At least 200 said killed in Indonesia clashes.

text.p: Ethnic clashes in Indonesia's West Kalimantan province early this year killed at least 200 people and caused 27,000 to flee the fighting between local Dayaks and migrant Madurese, the region's governor said on Thursday.

In the first official account of the violence which started in late December, West Kalimantan Governor Aswin Aspar said that as of March 21 about 14,000 people of those who fled had not yet returned home.

"The preliminary figure (for those killed) is already 200 people from both sides. We cannot identify from which group or from where they came," Aspar told reporters after meeting President Suharto in Jakarta.
"We are still making an inventory of the dead as there are some who have not yet been found because they were buried by their friends or by other people," he said.
He said the official National Commission of Human Rights would help with count the number of victims from the two incidents.

The first incident started on December 29 when Dayaks and Madurese clashed in Sanggau Ledo in a fight started over a girl. The second flared on January 24 after masked men attacked Dayak-run church facilities in the capital Pontianak.
Aspar said there were 11 clashes in all, including five large ones, in disturbances similar to ones in 1977 and 1982.

He did not comment on the number of people, mostly Dayaks, said to have been shot by the army after hundreds of troops from the military's elite strategic reserve were called in to quell the disturbance and protect those fleeing, mostly Madurese.
The government had previously announced a much lower number of victims, while residents had said the figure could be as high as a thousand.
After newspapers in February quoted a senior general as saying the number of dead was around 300, officials were quick to deny the figure.

Aspar said the fighting was based on "racial hatred" between the indigenous Dayaks and the migrants from the island of Madura off the coast of the main island of Java. He said there was no evidence to say it was caused by economic disparity.
Residents reported the often vicious attacks included acts of cannibalism and that Dayaks, known in the past as head hunters, decapitating Madurese and displaying the heads on bamboo sticks.
Forty-two percent of West Kalimantan's population is Dayak, 31 percent Malay, 11 percent ethnic Chinese and balance from a number of ethnic groups including Madurese.
Aspar said 174 people, mostly Dayaks were still in custody and were being processed.
He said figures showed 2,469 houses were burned and 93 seriously damaged while 24 four-wheeled vehicles, 34 motorbikes, 364 bicycles were also damaged.
The first clash caused 13.5 billion rupiah ($5.61 million) worth of damage and the cost of the second larger clash had not yet been calculated, he added.
